assessmentSummary.identity: From a stationary two-foot stance beside one declared collapsible low hurdle, take off from both feet together, clear the hurdle laterally once, land on both feet together in the marked zone, absorb under control, hold without an extra step or hop, exit safely, and reset fully.
currentCardFindings: The ground-only bilateral parent is already complete, but a raised obstacle adds equipment, minimum clearance, trip exposure, landing-location demand, and failure consequences that require a separate canonical definition.
The legacy low-hurdle source does not declare foot count and is not mapped to this authored card.
Five oEmbed-healthy title-level candidates remain unreviewed for exact movement, quality, safety, captions, accessibility, reviewer identity, and approval.

currentCardSnapshot.description: From a stationary two-foot stance beside one declared collapsible low hurdle, take off from both feet together, clear the hurdle laterally once, land on both feet together in the marked zone, absorb under control, hold without an extra step or hop, exit safely, and reset fully.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical differences between unilateral and bilateral landings from a jump
claims: Unilateral and bilateral landings have materially different knee kinematics and muscle-activation demands.
A lateral hurdle task must declare takeoff foot count, landing foot count and leg, obstacle, direction, contact count, terminal hold, and reset; hop or jump wording alone cannot supply those facts.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training specificity of hurdle vs. countermovement jump training
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Bilateral and unilateral hurdle jumps showed different force and contact-time characteristics in a standardized protocol.

Raised-hurdle clearance is represented separately from a floor-line or open-floor target because it adds required equipment, minimum clearance, visual demand, trip exposure, and altered failure consequences.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical differences between unilateral and bilateral landings from a jump
claims: Jump landing uses foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk control, with different demands when landing on one leg versus two.
Cards declare plantar flexors, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals, hip adductors and rotators, foot and ankle stabilizers, and trunk stabilizers without implying isolated-muscle causation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of hurdle height on lower limb joint kinematics and kinetics of male trainee sprinters during hurdle jumps
claims: Changing hurdle height altered jump height and flight-phase hip and knee positions in the studied hurdle-jump protocol.
The exact card fixes one lateral clearance, declared low obstacle dimensions, declared takeoff and landing support, controlled absorption, terminal hold, and full reset.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training specificity of hurdle vs. countermovement jump training
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Hurdle and support conditions change mechanical and coordination demands and therefore must remain fixed when comparing tasks.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of hurdle height on lower limb joint kinematics and kinetics of male trainee sprinters during hurdle jumps
claims: Hurdle height can alter clearance strategy even when some lower-limb work measures do not differ between tested heights.

Track obstacle dimensions, bodyweight contacts, takeoff and landing support, direction, landing quality, attempts, other jump and running load, symptoms, rest, and recovery without asserting a universal threshold.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of hurdle height on lower limb joint kinematics and kinetics of male trainee sprinters during hurdle jumps
claims: Obstacle dimensions are part of the task and cannot be treated as invisible equipment metadata.
Require a collapsible low hurdle, level high-traction surface, marked takeoff and landing zones, clear fall space, no cross-traffic, stable footwear policy, and a complete coach sightline.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Landing-feedback interventions use observable movement targets, but the evidence does not establish one universal safe repetition count.
Dose fully reset single clearances, count every landing contact and side, preserve the declared hold, and stop before technique or output changes.
Lateral line drills distinguish one-foot and two-foot execution and demonstrate why support must be named explicitly.
Instructions state foot support, direction, obstacle, takeoff zone, clearance, landing zone, whole-foot absorption, hold, exit, and reset.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of hurdle height on lower limb joint kinematics and kinetics of male trainee sprinters during hurdle jumps
claims: Hurdle height changes flight posture and must be selected deliberately rather than progressed by assumption.

Stop for pain, guarding, obstacle contact, toe catch, uncontrolled landing, split or wrong-foot contact, free-foot touch, extra hop or step, target miss, alignment loss, dizziness, unsafe equipment, or two changed reps.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training specificity of hurdle vs. countermovement jump training
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Bilateral and unilateral hurdle protocols have different mechanical characteristics and should not be pooled silently.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Clear observable landing feedback can support movement practice, but card text cannot promise injury prevention.
Athlete support explains the foot contract, obstacle, target, expected landing, symptoms, self-checks, stop rule, and how to request a ground-only or non-impact alternative.

claims: Standardized hurdle protocols require the support condition and obstacle setup to remain consistent.
Coaches document hurdle dimensions, takeoff and landing marks, foot contract, direction, valid attempts, contacts, hold, rest, side order, faults, symptoms, and substitutions.

claims: Changing from unilateral to bilateral landing changes the task rather than merely reducing difficulty.
